intro.title: Text functions
intro.bodyMarkdown:
This quest uses a new database: a small online shop's `customers`, `orders` and `employees`. Open **Tables** to see the columns. Like most real data, it's a little messy: some names are typed in odd cases, and some cities have extra spaces around them.

A **function** takes values in brackets and gives back a new value. Text functions change or measure text:

```
SELECT first_name, UPPER(first_name) AS upper_name, LOWER(email) AS email
FROM customers;
```

`UPPER(text)` gives capitals, `LOWER(text)` small letters, and `LENGTH(text)` the number of characters, spaces included. Like calculations, functions change only the result, never the table, and a function given `NULL` gives `NULL` back.

`TRIM(text)` removes spaces from both ends; `LTRIM` and `RTRIM` remove them from the left or the right only. `LENGTH(' Lagos')` is 6, and `LENGTH(TRIM(' Lagos'))` is 5.

Functions can go inside each other. The innermost one is worked out first:

```
SELECT UPPER(TRIM(city)) AS city FROM customers;
```

Functions work in `WHERE` and `ORDER BY` too. `=` is case-sensitive, so comparing in one case finds every spelling: `WHERE LOWER(first_name) = 'ben'` finds `ben`, `Ben` and `BEN`.

Text joined with `||` can include function results: `first_name || ' ' || UPPER(last_name)`.

intro.title: Parts of text
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`SUBSTR(text, start, length)` takes part of a text. Positions count from **1**, so `SUBSTR(joined, 1, 4)` is the first four characters of a date like `2024-02-14`: the year.

```
SELECT joined, SUBSTR(joined, 1, 4) AS year, SUBSTR(joined, 6, 2) AS month
FROM customers;
```

Leave out the length to take everything from `start` to the end. A negative start counts from the end: `SUBSTR(phone, -4)` is the last four characters.

`INSTR(text, part)` finds where `part` first appears, or gives 0 if it doesn't. `INSTR('ana@example.com', '@')` is 4.

`REPLACE(text, old, new)` swaps every `old` for `new`: `REPLACE('555-0101', '-', '')` is `5550101`. It is case-sensitive.

Together they can cut text at a marker. The part of an email before the `@` ends one character before it, and the domain starts one character after it:

```
SELECT email,
  SUBSTR(email, 1, INSTR(email, '@') - 1) AS username,
  SUBSTR(email, INSTR(email, '@') + 1) AS domain
FROM customers;
```

With `UPPER` and `LOWER`, you can fix the capitals of a name: a capital first letter, `UPPER(SUBSTR(first_name, 1, 1))`, then the rest in small letters, `LOWER(SUBSTR(first_name, 2))`.

intro.title: Numbers and rounding
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`ROUND(x)` rounds to a whole number and `ROUND(x, 2)` to two decimal places. Halves round away from zero, so `ROUND(2.5)` is 3. The result keeps a decimal point: `ROUND(42.5)` shows as `43.0`.

`CEIL(x)` always rounds **up** to the next whole number and `FLOOR(x)` always rounds **down**: `CEIL(15.01)` is 16 and `FLOOR(15.99)` is 15. Use them when rounding the usual way would be wrong, such as counting how many boxes you need.

`ABS(x)` drops the minus sign, which is handy for "how far apart": `ABS(total - 100)` is the distance from 100 either way.

```
SELECT id, total, ROUND(total) AS rounded, CEIL(total) AS up, FLOOR(total) AS down
FROM orders;
```

Remember whole-number division from the last quest: `salary / 12` drops the decimals because both numbers are whole. Divide by `12.0` to keep them, and round the result: `ROUND(salary / 12.0, 2)`.

`%` gives the **remainder** of a division: `7 % 2` is 1. A number is even when `x % 2 = 0`, and `x % 10` is its last digit.

Percentages work as in maths: a 15% discount on a total is `total * 15 / 100.0`, and what is left to pay is `total * (100 - 15) / 100.0`.

intro.title: CASE: choosing a value
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`CASE` chooses a value for each row, like an IF in other programming languages. It checks its `WHEN` conditions in order and uses the value after the first one that is true; if none is, it uses the `ELSE` value. It ends with `END`.

```
SELECT id, total,
  CASE WHEN total >= 100 THEN 'big' ELSE 'small' END AS size
FROM orders;
```

There can be as many `WHEN`s as you need. Because the first true one wins, put the strictest condition first:

```
SELECT name, salary,
  CASE
    WHEN salary >= 60000 THEN 'high'
    WHEN salary >= 40000 THEN 'medium'
    ELSE 'low'
  END AS band
FROM employees;
```

A salary of 65500 is also at least 40000, but it gets `'high'` because that `WHEN` comes first. In the other order, nobody would ever be `'high'`.

Without an `ELSE`, rows that match no `WHEN` get `NULL`.

When every condition compares the same column with `=`, there is a shorter form: name the column after `CASE` and give only values after each `WHEN`.

```
SELECT id,
  CASE status WHEN 'shipped' THEN 'Sent' WHEN 'pending' THEN 'Waiting' ELSE 'Cancelled' END AS label
FROM orders;
```

Like any other column, a `CASE` column needs a name given with `AS`.

intro.title: Sorting and filtering with CASE
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`CASE` is an expression, so it can go anywhere a value can: in `ORDER BY`, in `WHERE`, and inside calculations.

**A custom order.** Alphabetical order isn't always what you want. To show pending orders first, sort by a number that `CASE` gives each row:

```
SELECT id, status FROM orders
ORDER BY CASE WHEN status = 'pending' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END, id;
```

Pending orders get 0 and the rest get 1, so the pending ones come first; `id` then orders each group. The numbers themselves aren't shown.

**Different rules for different rows.** A `CASE` inside a calculation lets each row use its own rule. Here support staff get a 10% rise and everyone else 5%:

```
SELECT name, salary,
  ROUND(salary * CASE WHEN role = 'Support' THEN 1.10 ELSE 1.05 END) AS new_salary
FROM employees;
```

**Filtering on a worked-out value.** In `WHERE`, a `CASE` can work out the value to compare. This finds orders worth more than 100 after their discount, treating a missing discount as none:

```
SELECT id, total, discount FROM orders
WHERE CASE WHEN discount IS NULL THEN total
           ELSE total * (100 - discount) / 100.0 END > 100;
```

Dates written as `YYYY-MM-DD` compare correctly as text, because the year comes first: `hire_date < '2020-01-01'` means "hired before 2020". The next stages do much more with dates.

intro.title: Replacing NULL
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A missing value spreads: a calculation with `NULL` in it gives `NULL`. `salary + bonus` is `NULL` for anyone without a bonus, and `first_name || ' from ' || city` is `NULL` when the city is missing. Often you'd rather use a stand-in value.

`COALESCE(a, b, …)` gives the first of its values that is not `NULL`. With a value as the last argument, the result is never `NULL`:

```
SELECT name, salary + COALESCE(bonus, 0) AS total_pay FROM employees;
```

`COALESCE(phone, email)` gives the phone number when there is one, and the email otherwise. `COALESCE(phone, email, 'no contact')` adds a last resort.

`IFNULL(a, b)` does the same with exactly two values: `IFNULL(bonus, 0)`. `COALESCE` is standard SQL and works in every database, so this course mostly uses it.

`NULLIF(a, b)` goes the other way: it gives `NULL` when `a` equals `b`, and `a` otherwise. `NULLIF(discount, 0)` treats a discount of 0 as "no discount". It also prevents dividing by zero, because dividing by `NULL` gives `NULL` instead of a wrong answer: `total / NULLIF(quantity, 0)`.

A stand-in is for showing or calculating, not for pretending: in `WHERE`, `discount IS NULL` still tells you which rows really have no value.

intro.title: Dates
intro.bodyMarkdown:
SQLite has no separate date type: dates are usually stored as text in the form `YYYY-MM-DD`, such as `2026-03-01`. That form is chosen on purpose. With the year first, then the month, then the day, sorting the text alphabetically also sorts the dates, and comparisons work too:

```
SELECT id, order_date FROM orders
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-31'
ORDER BY order_date;
```

Months and days always have two digits (`03`, not `3`): without them, `'2026-10-02'` would sort before `'2026-9-28'`.

`strftime(format, date)` takes the parts you want out of a date, as text. `%Y` is the year, `%m` the month, `%d` the day, `%w` the day of the week (`0` is Sunday, `6` is Saturday) and `%j` the day of the year. Other characters are kept as they are:

```
SELECT order_date,
  strftime('%Y', order_date) AS year,
  strftime('%m', order_date) AS month,
  strftime('%d/%m/%Y', order_date) AS written
FROM orders;
```

Because the parts are text, compare them with text: `strftime('%Y', joined) = '2024'`, or `strftime('%w', order_date) IN ('0', '6')` for weekends.

`date(text)` gives a date in the standard form (or `NULL` if the text isn't a date). `date('now')` is today's date, but its result changes every day, so the challenges here use fixed dates.

intro.title: Date arithmetic
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`date(date, modifier, …)` moves a date. Modifiers like `'+7 days'`, `'-1 month'` or `'+1 year'` add or take away time, and SQLite handles the different lengths of months and leap years:

```
SELECT order_date,
  date(order_date, '+7 days') AS due,
  date(order_date, '+1 month') AS next_month
FROM orders;
```

`'start of month'` goes back to the 1st of the month. Modifiers apply in order, so `date(d, 'start of month', '+1 month', '-1 day')` is the last day of `d`'s month.

**How far apart?** `julianday(date)` turns a date into a number of days, so subtracting two of them gives the days in between:

```
SELECT id, julianday(ship_date) - julianday(order_date) AS days_to_ship
FROM orders WHERE ship_date IS NOT NULL;
```

The result can have decimals (it counts time of day too), so it shows as `2.0`. For dates without times it is always a whole number of days.

Comparisons and modifiers combine: `ship_date <= date(order_date, '+1 day')` means "shipped by the next day".

Challenges use the fixed date `'2026-10-24'` as "today" so their answers don't change. In real queries you would write `date('now')`.

For whole years, divide the days by 365.25 (counting leap years) and round down: `FLOOR((julianday('2026-10-24') - julianday(hire_date)) / 365.25)`.

intro.title: Types and CAST
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Every value has a **type**. SQLite has five: `integer` (whole numbers), `real` (numbers with decimals), `text`, `blob` (raw bytes, such as images) and `null`. `typeof(value)` tells you which one a value is:

```
SELECT id, typeof(total) AS total_type, typeof(discount) AS discount_type,
       typeof(order_date) AS date_type
FROM orders;
```

SQLite is flexible about types, but the type still matters. Text sorts letter by letter, so as text `'9'` comes after `'10'` (9 is bigger than 1). Numbers stored or produced as text, like the results of `strftime` and `SUBSTR`, sort and compare the text way.

`CAST(value AS type)` turns a value into another type. `CAST('09' AS INTEGER)` is the number 9; `CAST(salary AS TEXT)` is text; `CAST(5 AS REAL)` is 5.0.

```
SELECT order_date, CAST(strftime('%m', order_date) AS INTEGER) AS month FROM orders;
```

`CAST(x AS INTEGER)` **cuts off** the decimals instead of rounding: `CAST(42.99 AS INTEGER)` is 42, while `ROUND(42.99)` is 43.0. That also makes it a way to drop the `.0` that `ROUND` leaves: `CAST(ROUND(42.99) AS INTEGER)` is 43.

Some things that look like numbers should stay text: phone numbers, postcodes and ID codes like `007` would lose their leading zeros as numbers, and you never do maths with them.

intro.title: Formatting with printf
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`printf(format, values…)` builds text from a pattern. Each `%` code in the pattern is replaced by the next value: `%s` for text, `%d` for a whole number and `%f` for a number with decimals. Everything else is copied as it is.

```
SELECT printf('%s works as %s', name, role) AS line FROM employees;
```

Between the `%` and the letter you can say how the value should look. `%.2f` always shows two decimals, so `printf('%.2f', 42.5)` is `42.50`, which `ROUND` can't do: `ROUND(42.5, 2)` is still 42.5.

A number before the letter sets a minimum width, padded with spaces: `%5d`. Starting it with 0 pads with zeros: `printf('ORD-%04d', 7)` is `ORD-0007`. A comma adds thousands separators: `printf('%,d', 72000)` is `72,000`. To write a real percent sign, use `%%`.

```
SELECT printf('ORD-%04d', id) AS order_no, printf('%.2f', total) AS total,
       printf('%d%%', discount) AS discount
FROM orders;
```

`printf` gives **text**. That is right for showing results, but sort by the original numbers: as text, `100.00` comes before `9.50`.

SQLite also calls this function `format` in newer versions; `printf` works in all of them.

intro.title: Easy side quest: Customer clean-up
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The shop is sending its first newsletter, and the `customers` table needs tidying first: names in odd capitals, spaces around cities, emails in mixed case and missing phone numbers.

You won't change the table itself (that comes in a later quest). Instead, each challenge builds part of a clean list, and the last one puts it all together.

You'll need `TRIM`, `UPPER`, `LOWER`, `SUBSTR`, `INSTR`, `COALESCE` and `||`.
intro.sandboxCode: SELECT first_name, last_name, email, city, phone FROM customers;

challenges.title: Easy: Emails, cleaned
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each customer's `id` and their email in lower case, called `email`, in order of `id`.
challenges.hint: `LOWER(email) AS email ... ORDER BY id`.
challenges.solution: SELECT id, LOWER(email) AS email FROM customers ORDER BY id;

challenges.title: Easy: Cities, cleaned
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each customer's `id` and their city without extra spaces, or `unknown` if it is missing, called `city`.
challenges.hint: `COALESCE(TRIM(city), 'unknown') AS city`.
challenges.solution: SELECT id, COALESCE(TRIM(city), 'unknown') AS city FROM customers;

challenges.title: Medium: Names, cleaned
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each customer's `id`, and their first and last names each with a capital first letter and the rest in small letters, called `first_name` and `last_name`.
challenges.hint: Do the same for both: `UPPER(SUBSTR(x, 1, 1)) || LOWER(SUBSTR(x, 2))`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT id,
  UPPER(SUBSTR(first_name, 1, 1)) || LOWER(SUBSTR(first_name, 2)) AS first_name,
  UPPER(SUBSTR(last_name, 1, 1)) || LOWER(SUBSTR(last_name, 2)) AS last_name
FROM customers;

challenges.title: Medium: Phones
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each customer's `id` and their phone number, or `none` when it is missing, called `phone`.
challenges.hint: `COALESCE(phone, 'none') AS phone`.
challenges.solution: SELECT id, COALESCE(phone, 'none') AS phone FROM customers;

challenges.title: Hard: Email domains
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each customer's `id` and the part of their email after the `@`, in lower case, called `domain`. Sort by domain, then by `id`.
challenges.hint: `LOWER(SUBSTR(email, INSTR(email, '@') + 1)) AS domain ... ORDER BY domain, id`.
challenges.solution: SELECT id, LOWER(SUBSTR(email, INSTR(email, '@') + 1)) AS domain FROM customers ORDER BY domain, id;

challenges.title: Hard: The mailing list
challenges.promptMarkdown: Put it all together: one column called `entry` like `Ben Okafor <ben.okafor@example.com>, Lagos`, with proper capitals, a lower-case email and the trimmed city (or `unknown`). Sort by the cleaned last name, then first name.
challenges.hint: Build the name parts as before, join them with `||`, and sort by the same cleaned expressions (or by `LOWER(last_name), LOWER(first_name)`).
challenges.solution:
SELECT UPPER(SUBSTR(first_name, 1, 1)) || LOWER(SUBSTR(first_name, 2)) || ' ' ||
       UPPER(SUBSTR(last_name, 1, 1)) || LOWER(SUBSTR(last_name, 2)) ||
       ' <' || LOWER(email) || '>, ' || COALESCE(TRIM(city), 'unknown') AS entry
FROM customers
ORDER BY LOWER(last_name), LOWER(first_name);

intro.title: Medium side quest: Order tracker
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The shop wants a page that tracks its `orders`: what state each one is in, how long shipping took, what customers actually paid, and which orders are still waiting.

Take "today" to be 2026-10-24. A missing discount means no discount; a missing ship date means the order hasn't shipped.

You'll use `CASE`, `COALESCE`, `julianday`, `strftime` and `printf`.
intro.sandboxCode: SELECT id, order_date, ship_date, total, discount, status FROM orders;

challenges.title: Easy: Order states
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each order's `id` and a `state`: `on its way` for shipped orders, `to send` for pending ones and `cancelled` for cancelled ones. In order of `id`.
challenges.hint: `CASE status WHEN 'shipped' THEN 'on its way' WHEN 'pending' THEN 'to send' ELSE 'cancelled' END AS state ... ORDER BY id`.

challenges.title: Easy: Amount paid
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each order's `id` and the amount paid after any discount, with two decimals as text (`42.50`), called `paid`.
challenges.hint: `printf('%.2f', total * (100 - COALESCE(discount, 0)) / 100.0) AS paid`.
challenges.solution: SELECT id, printf('%.2f', total * (100 - COALESCE(discount, 0)) / 100.0) AS paid FROM orders;

challenges.title: Medium: Shipping speed
challenges.promptMarkdown: For the shipped orders, show the `id`, the days it took to ship as a whole number (`days`), and `speed`: `fast` for 2 days or less, `slow` otherwise. Slowest first; equal days in `id` order.
challenges.hint: `CAST(julianday(ship_date) - julianday(order_date) AS INTEGER) AS days`, then `CASE WHEN ... <= 2 THEN 'fast' ELSE 'slow' END`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT id,
  CAST(julianday(ship_date) - julianday(order_date) AS INTEGER) AS days,
  CASE WHEN julianday(ship_date) - julianday(order_date) <= 2 THEN 'fast' ELSE 'slow' END AS speed
FROM orders
WHERE ship_date IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY days DESC, id;

challenges.title: Medium: Still waiting
challenges.promptMarkdown: For the `pending` orders, show the `id`, `order_date` and how many whole days each has waited by 2026-10-24 (`waiting`). Longest wait first.
challenges.hint: `CAST(julianday('2026-10-24') - julianday(order_date) AS INTEGER) AS waiting ... ORDER BY waiting DESC`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT id, order_date, CAST(julianday('2026-10-24') - julianday(order_date) AS INTEGER) AS waiting
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY waiting DESC;

challenges.title: Hard: Monthly labels
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each order's `id` and a `label` like `2026-03 #5: 230.75` (the year and month of the order, a # and the id, then the total with two decimals). Sort by `order_date`.
challenges.hint: `printf('%s #%d: %.2f', strftime('%Y-%m', order_date), id, total) AS label ... ORDER BY order_date`.

challenges.title: Hard: The tracker
challenges.promptMarkdown: Put it together for the orders that aren't cancelled: `id`, `order_date`, `paid` (after discount, rounded to 2 decimals, as a number) and `shipping`: the ship date, or `waiting 22 days` for unshipped orders (whole days up to 2026-10-24). Newest order first.
challenges.hint: `COALESCE(ship_date, printf('waiting %d days', CAST(julianday('2026-10-24') - julianday(order_date) AS INTEGER))) AS shipping`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT id, order_date,
  ROUND(total * (100 - COALESCE(discount, 0)) / 100.0, 2) AS paid,
  COALESCE(ship_date, printf('waiting %d days', CAST(julianday('2026-10-24') - julianday(order_date) AS INTEGER))) AS shipping
FROM orders
WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
ORDER BY order_date DESC;

intro.title: Hard side quest: Staff report
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The manager needs a staff report from the `employees` table: years of service, pay bands, monthly pay, bonuses and a one-line summary for each person.

Take "today" to be 2026-10-24. A missing bonus means no bonus.

This side quest uses the whole quest: text functions, numbers, `CASE`, `COALESCE`, dates, `CAST` and `printf`.
intro.sandboxCode: SELECT name, role, salary, hire_date, bonus FROM employees;

challenges.title: Easy: Years of service
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each employee's `name` and their whole years of service by 2026-10-24, called `years`, as a whole number. Most years first; equal values in name order.
challenges.hint: `CAST((julianday('2026-10-24') - julianday(hire_date)) / 365.25 AS INTEGER) AS years`.

challenges.title: Easy: Pay bands
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each employee's `name`, `salary` and `band`: `A` for 65000 or more, `B` for 50000 or more, `C` for 35000 or more, and `D` otherwise. Highest salary first.
challenges.hint: Strictest first: `CASE WHEN salary >= 65000 THEN 'A' WHEN salary >= 50000 THEN 'B' WHEN salary >= 35000 THEN 'C' ELSE 'D' END`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT name, salary,
  CASE
    WHEN salary >= 65000 THEN 'A'
    WHEN salary >= 50000 THEN 'B'
    WHEN salary >= 35000 THEN 'C'
    ELSE 'D'
  END AS band
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC;

challenges.title: Medium: Monthly pay
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each employee's `name` and their monthly pay (salary plus any bonus, divided by 12) with exactly two decimals, like `6416.67`, called `monthly`.
challenges.hint: `printf('%.2f', (salary + COALESCE(bonus, 0)) / 12.0) AS monthly`. Without COALESCE, anyone without a bonus would get NULL.
challenges.solution: SELECT name, printf('%.2f', (salary + COALESCE(bonus, 0)) / 12.0) AS monthly FROM employees;

challenges.title: Medium: Initials and role
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show one column called `badge` like `ML - MANAGER`: the initials of each employee, a dash with a space on each side, and the role in capitals.
challenges.hint: `SUBSTR(name, 1, 1) || SUBSTR(name, INSTR(name, ' ') + 1, 1) || ' - ' || UPPER(role) AS badge`.
challenges.solution: SELECT SUBSTR(name, 1, 1) || SUBSTR(name, INSTR(name, ' ') + 1, 1) || ' - ' || UPPER(role) AS badge FROM employees;

challenges.title: Hard: Anniversaries this year
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each employee's `name` and the date of their work anniversary in 2026, called `anniversary` (the month and day they were hired, in 2026). Sort by that date.
challenges.hint: `'2026' || SUBSTR(hire_date, 5) AS anniversary ... ORDER BY anniversary`. (SUBSTR from position 5 is `-MM-DD`.)
challenges.solution: SELECT name, '2026' || SUBSTR(hire_date, 5) AS anniversary FROM employees ORDER BY anniversary;

challenges.title: Hard: The report
challenges.promptMarkdown: One `line` per employee like `Maria Lopez, Manager since 2015 (11 years): 72,000 + 5,000 bonus`. Use `+ no bonus` when there is none. Most years first; equal years in name order.
challenges.hint: Build the line with printf: `printf('%s, %s since %s (%d years): %,d + %s', name, role, strftime('%Y', hire_date), <years>, salary, <bonus part>)`. For the bonus part use CASE, because printf turns a NULL number into 0: `CASE WHEN bonus IS NULL THEN 'no bonus' ELSE printf('%,d bonus', bonus) END`. Sort by the years expression DESC, then name.
challenges.solution:
SELECT printf('%s, %s since %s (%d years): %,d + %s',
    name, role, strftime('%Y', hire_date),
    CAST((julianday('2026-10-24') - julianday(hire_date)) / 365.25 AS INTEGER),
    salary,
    CASE WHEN bonus IS NULL THEN 'no bonus' ELSE printf('%,d bonus', bonus) END) AS line
FROM employees
ORDER BY CAST((julianday('2026-10-24') - julianday(hire_date)) / 365.25 AS INTEGER) DESC, name;

questions.prompt: Why divide the days by 365.25 for years of service?
questions.explanation: Every fourth year has 366 days, so a year is about 365.25 days on average.
.2 keeps two decimals, rounding the last one. (The comma flag only works with %d.)

questions.prompt: Which band does a salary of 50000 get with `>= 65000 A, >= 50000 B, >= 35000 C`?
questions.explanation: 50000 is not 65000 or more, but it is 50000 or more.
Everything from position 5 to the end.

questions.prompt: Why sort the report by hire date for "most years first"?

choices.label: Earlier hires have more years of service

questions.explanation: The earliest hire date has the most years.

questions.prompt: What does `CASE WHEN bonus IS NULL THEN 'no bonus' ELSE printf('%,d bonus', bonus) END` give for a bonus of 2500?
questions.explanation: The bonus exists, so the ELSE part formats it.
